summary:
🤯 big update to our flow map language models paper!
we believe this is the future of non-autoregressive text generation.
read about it in the blog:
full details in the paper:
we introduce a new class of continuous flow-based language models and distill them into their corresponding flow map for one-step text generation.
we beat all discrete diffusion baselines at ~8x speed!
v2 gives a complete theory of the flow map over discrete data, with three equivalent ways to learn it (semigroup, lagrangian, eulerian). it turns out you can train these with cross-entropy objectives that look very similar to standard discrete diffusion — but without the factorization error that kills discrete methods at few steps.
beyond improving results across the board, we showcase properties that are unique to continuous flows. in particular, inference-time steering and guidance become straightforward. autoguidance brings generative perplexity down to 51.6 on LM1B, while discrete baselines completely collapse at the same guidance scale.
we also show reward-guided generation for steering topic, sentiment, grammaticality, and safety at inference time — and it works even at 1-2 steps with our flow map model. simple, well-understood techniques from continuous flows just work incredibly well in practice for language.
we’re extremely excited about the future of this class of models.
stay tuned for results on scaling, reasoning, and reinforcement learning-based fine-tuning. 🚀
🎬 https://pbs.twimg.com/amplify_video_thumb/2041544843524976640/img/6SHIDeVll8gw7PMl.jpg | https://video.twimg.com/amplify_video/2041544843524976640/vid/avc1/320x440/qMxYnIDv1j6varMJ.mp4?tag=21
clean_summary:
Big update to our flow map language models paper! We believe this is the future of non-autoregressive text generation. We introduce a new class of continuous flow-based language models and distill them into their corresponding flow map for one-step text generation, beating all discrete diffusion baselines at approximately eight times the speed.

Version 2 provides a complete theory of the flow map over discrete data, with three equivalent ways to learn it: semigroup, Lagrangian, and Eulerian. These can be trained with cross-entropy objectives similar to standard discrete diffusion, but without the factorization error that affects discrete methods at few steps. Beyond improving results, we showcase unique properties of continuous flows, such as straightforward inference-time steering and guidance. Autoguidance reduces generative perplexity to 51.6 on LM1B, while discrete baselines collapse at the same guidance scale. We also demonstrate reward-guided generation for steering topic, sentiment, grammaticality, and safety at inference time, effective even at one to two steps with our flow map model. Simple techniques from continuous flows work incredibly well in practice for language.

We’re excited about the future of this class of models and will share results on scaling, reasoning, and reinforcement learning-based fine-tuning.

clean_title: Introducing Introspective Diffusion Language Model (I-DLM)
summary:
🤔The more I studied diffusion language models, the more I came to appreciate the simplicity of autoregressive (AR) language models. AR models are trained to agree with what they generate, and their serving stacks are built to preserve that structure. DLMs often do neither: they lack introspective consistency, and high TPF does not necessarily translate into high real-world TPS.
We propose Introspective Diffusion Language Model (I-DLM), which unifies introspection and generation in a single pass:
1. 🧑‍🎓I-DLM brings introspective consistency to DLMs with only 5B training tokens, achieving AR-thinking-level quality.
2. 🚀 I-DLM carefully trades compute for higher TPF while converting that advantage into real TPS under high-concurrency serving.
📖Website:
⌨️Code:
🎬 https://pbs.twimg.com/amplify_video_thumb/2043873503091535873/img/nNRefnNoDuiQbDQd.jpg | https://video.twimg.com/amplify_video/2043873503091535873/vid/avc1/480x270/7ciMHBcF1ywaDrSl.mp4?tag=21
clean_summary:
The more I studied diffusion language models, the more I came to appreciate the simplicity of autoregressive (AR) language models. AR models are trained to agree with what they generate, and their serving stacks are built to preserve that structure. Diffusion language models (DLMs) often do neither; they lack introspective consistency, and high token per frame (TPF) does not necessarily translate into high real-world throughput per second (TPS).

I-DLM brings introspective consistency to DLMs with only 5 billion training tokens, achieving AR-thinking-level quality. It carefully trades compute for higher TPF while converting that advantage into real TPS under high-concurrency serving.

I-DLM is the first diffusion language model to match AR quality, achieving 69.6 on AIME-24 and 45.7 on LiveCodeBench-v6, outperforming LLaDA-2.1-mini (16B) with 2.9-4.1 times higher throughput.

title: Brandon Amos (@brandondamos)
clean_title: Reinforcement Learning from Rich Feedback with Distributional DAgger
summary:
A better teacher should improve the student. Right? 🤔
That’s the core bet behind on-policy self-distillation: Condition a model on rich feedback to get a strong teacher, then distill it back into the student.
In a new paper, we prove this can fail:
• Even with a strictly better teacher and exact natural-gradient updates, the broad class of 𝑓-divergence self-distillation objectives, including reverse KL and Jensen-Shannon, 𝗰𝗮𝗻 𝗺𝗮𝗸𝗲 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝘀𝘁𝘂𝗱𝗲𝗻𝘁 𝘄𝗼𝗿𝘀𝗲.
• Existing methods often only do local credit assignment: they look at where teacher and student disagree 𝘢𝘵 𝘦𝘢𝘤𝘩 𝘵𝘰𝘬𝘦𝘯. But early decisions shape future states. We prove that missing that future effect can lead to strictly suboptimal policies.

The paper introduces DistIL, a distributional variant of DAgger for reinforcement learning from rich feedback. clean_summary:
On-policy (self) distillation has a prefix failure issue: when the student's rollout is far from the teacher distribution, the teacher’s gradient signal becomes problematic. Trajectory-Refined Distillation (TRD) is introduced as a trajectory-level refinement of the student's output to address this problem.

The approach replaces traditional on-policy distillation with TRD, which improves the stability and effectiveness of the training process. The paper provides a detailed analysis and experimental results demonstrating the benefits of TRD over existing methods.

title: Brandon Amos (@brandondamos)
summary:
A super long overdue (3+ years?) post on scaling laws.
Compute is expensive. Scaling laws are a way to help us reason about the optimal compute allocation between data and model size before committing to a large run.
The post covers what scaling laws predict, how compute-optimal allocation works, why Kaplan et al. and Chinchilla disagree, and how data limits + fitting details make extrapolation tricky.

linked_urls.title: Scaling Laws, Carefully | Lil'Log
linked_urls.summary: Scaling laws are one of the most critical empirical findings in deep learning. The observation is simple in form: the training loss $L$ decreases predictably as we scale up model size $N$, dataset size $D$, and compute $C$, following a power-law curve, which appears as a straight line on a log-log plot. We can view scaling laws as a framework for describing the relationship between compute, loss, model size and data; at its core, it is about how to allocate precious compute optimally between $N$ and $D$.

new post on harness engineering for AI self-improvement:
It is hard to forecast how much the future of RSI will rely on harnesses. Likely harness engineering will evolve in the direction of self-improvement and enable auto-research, and, in turn, smarter models keeps harnesses simple.

linked_urls.title: Harness Engineering for Self-Improvement | Lil'Log
linked_urls.summary: The concept of recursive self-improvement (RSI) dates back to I. J. Good (1965), where he defined an “ultraintelligent machine” as a system that can surpass humans in all intellectual activities and design better machines to improve itself. Yudkowsky (2008) used the phrase “recursive self-improvement” for a specific feedback loop: an AI uses its current intelligence to improve the cognitive machinery that produces its intelligence. This feedback loop in modern AI may indicate the model rewriting its own weights directly, or more broadly the model improves the training pipeline and the deployment system, which in turn enables a better successor model with improved performance across economically valuable tasks. The speed of research development in AI has been shown to drastically accelerated in frontier labs (Anthropic; OpenAI).

New blog post: How to Build a Diffusion Language Model.
Diffusion LLMs went from open problem to reality in 2 years (Mercury, Gemma Diffusion, Nemotron Diffusion). With my Cornell group, we wrote up the research advances that make them work.
We use today's OSS large diffusion models as examples and show how they're built from core techniques:
• masked diffusion (MDLM)
• iterative refinement (UDLM, ReMDM)
• variable-length generation (block diffusion, encoder-decoder architectures)
• controllable generation (D-CFG, D-CBG)
• fast samplers (Duo)
• RL post-training (d1, d2)
This post covers research led by a talented group of Cornell PhD students including @mariannearr @SchiffYair @Guanghan__Wang
The content is adapted from talks I gave this year on dLLMs. It covers most of the main ingredients behind open-source diffusion language models today.

clean_title: DeepLoop: Depth Scaling for Looped Transformers
summary:
Crazy how looped/universal transformers are becoming popular now.
Back in 2018 when I independently discovered the universal transformer (which I called Recurrently Stacked Transformer), there was hardly any interest because people were not convinced that LLMs were really needed. One main observation is that looping through the same layer led to the representations being "refined" leading to their convergence to a particular value. But I was not smart enough to do the maths till someone else did.
A year later, I happened to come across @shaojieb's paper on deep equilibrium models who proposed a closed form solution to the converged representation due to looping, thereby saving compute costs. I had the honor of a brief interaction with him over this paper, where I shamelessly asked for my work on recurrently stacked transformers to be cited. 😅
Not sure if people have tried the closed form solution recently but I imagine it would be an interesting area to explore.
Strongly recommend reading this paper.

clean_summary:
Looped or universal transformers are gaining popularity. Back in 2018, the idea of recurrently stacking the same transformer layer was explored, showing that repeated passes refine representations until they converge, but the mathematical understanding was limited until a paper on deep equilibrium models proposed a closed-form solution for the converged state, which can save compute.

Recently, some frontier models are effectively 48-layer transformers looped twice, and DeepLoop introduces methods to make such looped transformers more stable and scalable. The linked arXiv paper provides a detailed study on depth scaling for these models, opening new avenues for efficient large-scale transformer design.
